extracted.intended_audience: parties and counsel in Trademark Trial and Appeal Board (TTAB) inter partes proceedings (trademark practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for conducting, resisting, and resolving discovery disputes in TTAB inter partes trademark proceedings, including when and how protective orders, depositions, interrogatories, requests for production, and conferences may be used or limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective order limiting or prohibiting depositions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board has discretion to limit a deposition or order that a deposition not be had if the discovery sought is obtainable from other sources that are more convenient and less burdensome or duplicative; the party seeking such an order bears the burden to show good cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Movant must submit a particular and specific demonstration of fact rather than stereotyped or conclusory statements. Lack of personal knowledge is generally insufficient to obtain a protective order; instead, showing that the party has no unique or superior personal knowledge and that others have equivalent or greater knowledge may support the order. Examples: protecting against exceeding the permitted ten depositions, preventing a second deposition of an individual, or stopping a deposition outside the discovery period. Assertions that a deponent is 'too busy' or that examination would cause undue labor, expense, or delay are generally insufficient. (Notes and case citations provided.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective orders for high-level officials/executives
rubrics_metrics.description: A movant seeking to prohibit deposition of a very high-level official or executive must demonstrate by affidavit or other evidence that the official has no direct knowledge of relevant facts or that others have equal or greater knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If movant meets initial burden, burden shifts to party seeking deposition to show the official has unique or superior personal knowledge; if not satisfied, Board will grant the protective order and require use of less intrusive methods (e.g., lower-level employee depositions, Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(b)(6) depositions, requests for admissions, interrogatories, requests for production). After a good-faith effort to use less intrusive methods, a party may move to vacate/modify the protective order by showing (1) a reasonable indication the deposition may lead to admissible evidence, and (2) that less intrusive methods are unsatisfactory, insufficient or inadequate. Board may nevertheless limit topics/duration (e.g., three hours, one topic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective orders based on medical or health grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: A party moving for a protective order to delay, limit, or prevent a deposition on medical or health grounds must make a specific and documented factual showing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General or conclusory assertions of health problems are insufficient; documentary or affidavit evidence is required to establish good cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for motions for protective orders
rubrics_metrics.description: The party seeking a protective order bears the burden to show good cause and must provide particular and specific facts, not conclusory statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(c)(1) and case law requiring a factual showing; if initial burden met in some contexts (e.g., high-level official), burden may shift to the party seeking discovery to show unique knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper use of protective orders as discovery response or harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: Except where discovery requests are so oppressive as to constitute clear harassment, it is generally improper to respond to a discovery request by filing a motion for protective order; it is also improper to move for a protective order to delay discovery or harass an adversary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The appropriate remedy for excessive interrogatories is to serve a general objection rather than seek a protective order. See TBMP §§ 405, 406 for proper responses and TBMP §§ 412, 526 for motions for protective orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board may deny or limit discovery requests that are oppressive or duplicative
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may order that discovery requested not be had with regard to interrogatories, requests for production, and requests for admission if the requests are oppressive, harassing, duplicative, or otherwise unjustified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board must assess whether protection is needed as to particular interrogatories or document categories due to their nature or volume. Examples include granting protective order for duplicative requests and denying for requests tailored to the issues. See case law examples (e.g., Phillies v. Philadelphia Consolidated Holding Corp.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of proportionality and duty to confer in discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties are expected to take into account proportionality for document requests and requests for admission, considering scope, and to confer in good faith about proper scope of discovery pursuant to 37 CFR § 2.120(a) and Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duty to cooperate is emphasized to minimize need for motions; see TBMP §§ 402 and 408 regarding scope of discovery and discovery conference obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telephone conferences to resolve discovery motions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may resolve or address stipulations or motions, including discovery motions, by telephone conference when resolution by correspondence is impractical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Telephone conferences expedite resolution and encourage cooperation; in appropriate cases the Board may indicate a responsive brief is unnecessary because the non-moving party can present arguments during the conference. The Board may require parties to contact the assigned attorney before filing discovery motions. Motions that have been decided by teleconference and related examples are cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pretrial conferences in person for complex interlocutory issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Where interlocutory issues have become so complex that resolution by correspondence or telephone conference is not practical, the Board may request or order an in-person pretrial conference in its offices with the parties or their attorneys.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rarely utilized but within Board discretion; Board may order in-person conferences where necessary to facilitate resolution without undue hardship to any party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of discovery documents not privileged
rubrics_metrics.description: The identification of discovery documents (as opposed to their substance) is not privileged or confidential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying documents does not waive privilege as to substance; case law citations support the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative sampling when full compliance is unduly burdensome
rubrics_metrics.description: When complete compliance with a discovery request would be unduly burdensome, the Board may permit compliance by providing a representative sampling or other reduced amount sufficient to meet the propounding party's discovery needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include producing representative invoices or samples by quarter; but if full production would not be burdensome, representative sampling may be inappropriate. Case law provides examples and limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discoverability of customer information: classes vs. names
rubrics_metrics.description: Classes of customers for involved goods or services are discoverable; the names of customers (including dealers) are generally confidential and not discoverable, even under protective order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: name of the first customer and, if relevant to abandonment, names of a minimal number of customers for the period may be discoverable under protective order. Case law and notes discuss balancing harm vs. need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discoverability of selection and adoption of an involved mark
rubrics_metrics.description: Information concerning a party's selection and adoption of its involved mark is generally discoverable (particularly of a defendant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identification of persons who suggested use of the mark or materials relating to selection are discoverable; limits exist where requests seek irrelevant third-party considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discoverability of first use information
rubrics_metrics.description: Information concerning a party's first use of its involved mark is discoverable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dates, locations, and identifying information about first use are pertinent to priority claims; case citations show scope of discovery required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search reports discoverable; attorney comments privileged
rubrics_metrics.description: Search reports are discoverable, but comments or opinions of attorneys relating to the search reports are privileged and not discoverable unless privilege is waived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce the factual search report; withhold privilege-protected attorney analysis. Case law distinguishing factual reports from privileged attorney work product is cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pretrial witness disclosure requirements (post-November 1, 2007)
rubrics_metrics.description: For proceedings commenced on or after November 1, 2007, pretrial disclosures must name witnesses expected to testify (or who may testify), provide general identifying information including phone/address, a general summary of subjects expected to be testified about, and a general summary/list of documents that may be introduced during testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a party expects to call no witnesses during its assigned testimony period it must state so; identity of such witnesses is therefore discoverable. Parties need not supplement initial disclosures to provide identifying information if it was previously made known in writing or during discovery. For proceedings before Nov. 1, 2007, advance witness identification was generally not required except for experts. Regardless of commencement date, parties need not pre-disclose each document they plan to introduce at trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plans for expansion may be discoverable under protective order
rubrics_metrics.description: A party's plans for expansion (business plans) may be discoverable, subject to protective order to protect confidentiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure may be limited under protective order depending on sensitivity; case law provides examples where expansion plans were deemed discoverable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discoverability of actual knowledge of third-party uses/registrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Information concerning a party's awareness of third-party use and/or registration of the same or similar marks is discoverable to the extent the responding party has actual knowledge (without conducting an investigation) and the information is reasonably calculated to lead to admissible evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no duty to conduct an investigation of third-party uses in response to discovery requests; only actual knowledge is required. Case law is cited for the no-investigation principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discoverability of litigation, settlement, and contractual agreements relating to mark
rubrics_metrics.description: Information concerning litigation and controversies, including settlement and other contractual agreements between a responding party and third parties based on the responding party's involved mark, is discoverable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required information about a legal proceeding is limited to names of the parties, jurisdiction, proceeding number, outcome, and citation of decision (if published). Parties need not provide all documents pertaining to the litigation beyond these basics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrelevance of marks/goods not involved in the proceeding
rubrics_metrics.description: A party need not provide discovery about marks and goods not involved in the proceeding and having no relevance thereto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, information showing that a party sells the same goods as the propounding party, even under a different mark, may be relevant to likelihood of confusion and thus discoverable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discoverability of names/addresses of officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Names and addresses of a party's officers are discoverable; if a party has many officers, it need only provide names/addresses of those most knowledgeable about the involved activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing the reasonable number of most knowledgeable individuals satisfies the obligation; case law supports identifying vice-presidents or equivalent as sufficient in many cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign use generally not discoverable but exceptions exist
rubrics_metrics.description: Information concerning a party's foreign use of its involved mark is usually irrelevant to Board proceedings and thus not discoverable, but exceptions arise (e.g., where adoption in U.S. was made in bad faith to forestall a foreign user's expansion, or where foreign mark is famous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law illustrates exceptions, including situations involving bad faith adoption or famous foreign marks. Generally foreign use creates no rights in the U.S. absent special circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stockholders' identities generally not discoverable
rubrics_metrics.description: Names and addresses of stockholders or entities owned/controlled by a party are generally irrelevant and not discoverable, unless there is a question whether the party and another entity are related companies under Trademark Act § 5, 15 U.S.C. § 1055.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only when related-company status is at issue will stockholder information become relevant and discoverable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locations of places of business where involved goods are manufactured or services conducted
rubrics_metrics.description: Locations of places of business where a party manufactures its involved goods or conducts its involved services under its involved mark are discoverable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such information is relevant to issues of use in commerce and marketplace presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Areas of distribution for involved goods or services discoverable
rubrics_metrics.description: Information relating to the areas of distribution for a party's involved goods or services sold under its involved mark is discoverable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geographic distribution data informs questions like market overlap and likelihood of confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of advertising agency and knowledgeable employees discoverable
rubrics_metrics.description: The identity of any advertising agency engaged by a party to advertise/promote its involved goods or services, and the identities of advertising agency employees having the most knowledge, are discoverable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This information may be obtained to explore advertising strategies, consumer perception, and promotional history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual sales and advertising figures discoverable in round numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Annual sales and advertising figures, stated in round numbers, for a party's involved goods or services are proper matters for discovery; if confidential, disclosure may be under protective order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should provide rounded figures and may seek protective orders to maintain confidentiality where appropriate. Case law examples show permitted limitations and formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discoverability of defendant's actual knowledge of plaintiff's mark use
rubrics_metrics.description: Information concerning a defendant's actual knowledge of plaintiff's use of the plaintiff's involved mark (including when and under what circumstances the knowledge was acquired) is discoverable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This information bears on issues such as willfulness and priority; parties should produce details of how/when knowledge was obtained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical expertise of purchasers is discoverable
rubrics_metrics.description: Information concerning the technical expertise of purchasers of a party's products is relevant to likelihood of confusion and is discoverable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If purchasers are sophisticated technical buyers, the likelihood of confusion analysis may be affected; production of evidence on purchaser sophistication is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion or contention discovery requests are not per se objectionable
rubrics_metrics.description: A discovery request is not necessarily objectionable merely because it requires a party or witness to give an opinion or contention that relates to fact or the application of law to fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests seeking opinions or contentions should be evaluated for relevance and scope rather than categorically disallowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery into validity of pleaded registration not automatically objectionable
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere taking of discovery on matters concerning the validity of a pleaded registration is not objectionable on the basis that it constitutes a collateral attack on the registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may explore validity issues via discovery; other safeguards or relevance limitations may apply depending on circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discoverable categories where mark is generic, merely descriptive, or lacks acquired distinctiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: When it is asserted that a mark is generic, merely descriptive, or lacks acquired distinctiveness, the following categories are discoverable: (1) materials assessing, evaluating, or considering methods of describing the product category; (2) materials relating to the decision to offer the product to the extent they refer to the product category or marks used/considered containing the term; (3) materials assessing/evaluating/considering how to categorize, describe or define the product; and (4) materials reflecting consumer views or comments about the product offered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories help probe whether a term is generic or descriptive and whether distinctiveness has been acquired; case law cited elaborates scope and limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on discovery about choice of product name when term at issue is not included
rubrics_metrics.description: Information and documents relating to the choice of a particular product name need not be provided unless that name includes the term at issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests into broader naming strategy are not required if they do not relate to the specific term being challenged; case law supports narrowing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time to file brief in response to motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Except as provided otherwise, a brief in response to a motion shall be filed within fifteen days from date of service of the motion, unless another time is specified by the Board or extended by stipulation or order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 CFR § 2.127(a) sets the default 15-day response period; the Board can alter timing and may permit teleconference resolution in lieu of response briefs.
